atcoder:abc172_c.title: ABC172 C. Tsundoku
levels: You always read a prefix of desk A and a prefix of desk B. Once you fix how many books you take from A, what is the best you can do on B?

Prefix sums + two pointers (or binary search). As the number of books taken from A grows, the longest affordable prefix of B can only shrink, so a single pointer moving backwards is enough. Classic WA: forgetting the case of taking 0 books from A.

1. Build prefix sums SA[0..N] and SB[0..M] in 64-bit.
2. j = M. For i = 0..N: if SA[i] > K stop; while SB[j] > K − SA[i], decrement j; ans = max(ans, i + j).
3. Print ans. O(N + M).

atcoder:abc175_c.title: ABC175 C. Walking Takahashi
levels: Values go up to 10^15, so simulating every move is impossible. Walking toward 0 is clearly right until you would overshoot — what do the remaining moves do after that?
Work with |X|. Take q = min(K, |X| / D) steps toward zero. If moves remain, you can only bounce between r = |X| − qD and r − D, so only the parity of the remaining moves matters.

1. X = |X|.
2. q = min(K, X / D); X −= q·D; K −= q.
3. If K is even print X, else print D − X.
Never compute K·D directly — it overflows 64-bit. O(1).

atcoder:abc194_e.title: ABC194 E. Mex Min
levels: The minimum mex over all windows is some value x that is missing from at least one window. When is a value x missing from some window of length M?
x is absent from some length-M window exactly when two consecutive occurrences of x (counting virtual positions −1 and N) leave a gap of at least M cells. The answer is the smallest such x.

1. For every value record its positions; add sentinels −1 and N.
2. x qualifies if some gap next − prev − 1 ≥ M.
3. Print the smallest qualifying x in 0..N. O(N).
(Alternative: slide the window keeping counts and a set of missing values.)

atcoder:abc187_d.title: ABC187 D. Choose Me
levels: Start from the state where you give no speeches. How much does the vote difference change when you speak in one town — and does it depend on the other towns?
A speech in town i changes (Takahashi − Aoki) by 2·A_i + B_i, independently of every other town. So greedily take the towns with the largest 2·A_i + B_i.

1. diff = −ΣA_i.
2. Sort towns by 2·A_i + B_i descending.
3. Add values one by one, counting, until diff > 0 (strictly). Use 64-bit. O(N log N).

atcoder:abc121_d.title: ABC121 D. XOR World
levels: Like range sums, a range XOR can be built from two prefix values. Write out 0 ⊕ 1 ⊕ … ⊕ n for small n — do you see a pattern?
g(n) = 0 ⊕ 1 ⊕ … ⊕ n depends only on n mod 4: it is n, 1, n + 1, 0. Then the answer is g(B) ⊕ g(A − 1).

1. g(n): n%4 == 0 → n, 1 → 1, 2 → n + 1, 3 → 0; define g(−1) = 0.
2. Print g(B) ^ g(A − 1). Watch the A = 0 case. O(1).

atcoder:abc136_e.title: ABC136 E. Max GCD
levels: The operation never changes the total sum S. What does that tell you about any number that divides every element at the end?

Any answer d must divide S, and S has only about a thousand divisors — try them all. For a fixed d, each element is rounded down or up to a multiple of d; the cheapest plan rounds the largest residues up and the smallest down.

1. Enumerate divisors of S in O(√S).
2. For each d: r_i = A_i mod d, sorted ascending; t = Σr_i / d elements must be rounded up (the t largest). Cost = sum of the N − t smallest residues.
3. The largest d with cost ≤ K is the answer. O(√S + D·N log N).

atcoder:abc131_d.title: ABC131 D. Megalomania
levels: If finishing everything is possible, does the order matter? Try swapping two adjacent jobs whose deadlines are out of order.
Earliest-deadline-first is optimal (exchange argument). Sort by deadline and check that every prefix finishes in time.

Sort by B ascending; t = 0; for each job: t += A; if t > B print No. Otherwise print Yes.
Common WA: sorting by A instead of B. O(N log N).

atcoder:dp_f.title: DP F. LCS
levels: Computing the length is the classic part; this task asks you to print an actual string. Which information in the table tells you which move you made?
Standard LCS DP over prefixes, then reconstruct by walking backwards from the bottom-right corner, moving to a neighbour with the same value, or taking the character when you must move diagonally.

1. dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1 if s[i−1] == t[j−1], else max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]).
2. From (|s|, |t|): if dp[i][j] == dp[i−1][j] → i−−; else if dp[i][j] == dp[i][j−1] → j−−; else take s[i−1], i−−, j−−.
3. Reverse the collected characters. O(|s|·|t|). Storing strings inside the DP is the usual TLE/MLE.

atcoder:abc128_c.title: ABC128 C. Switches
levels: Look at the constraints first: N ≤ 10. How many on/off combinations of switches exist in total?
Bit brute force: there are only 2^N ≤ 1024 states. For each one, check every bulb's parity condition.

for mask in 0..2^N − 1: for each bulb, count the switches s in its list with bit (s − 1) set; the state is valid if count % 2 == p_i for every bulb → ans++.
Common WA: off-by-one on the 1-indexed switch numbers. O(2^N · N · M).

atcoder:abc146_c.title: ABC146 C. Buy an Integer
levels: If you can afford the integer N, can you also afford every smaller integer? Use that monotonicity.
The price A·N + B·d(N) only increases with N, so binary search the largest affordable N in [0, 10^9].

lo = 0, hi = 10^9 + 1. While hi − lo > 1: mid = (lo + hi) / 2; if A·mid + B·digits(mid) ≤ X then lo = mid else hi = mid. Print lo.
The shop sells nothing above 10^9 — exceeding that cap is the usual WA. Use 64-bit. O(log 10^9).

atcoder:arc096_a.title: ABC095 C. Half and Half
levels: Two AB-pizzas can replace one A-pizza and one B-pizza. How many AB-pizzas could it ever make sense to buy?
Try every even number 2k of AB-pizzas for k = 0 .. max(X, Y) and buy the rest individually. Buying more AB-pizzas than you strictly need can be optimal when C is cheap.
ans = min over k in [0, max(X, Y)] of 2k·C + max(0, X − k)·A + max(0, Y − k)·B. O(max(X, Y)).

atcoder:abc085_d.title: ABC085 D. Katana Thrower
levels: You only ever need to wield one katana — which one? And when is a single throw better than wielding?
Let amax = max a_i. Throw every katana with b_i > amax, largest first, until the monster dies; then wield the best katana for the remaining damage.

1. amax = max a.
2. Sort b descending; for each b > amax: H −= b, cnt++; if H ≤ 0 print cnt.
3. Otherwise print cnt + ceil(H / amax). O(N log N).

codeforces:1934A.title: 1934A · Too Min Too Max
levels: The four chosen indices form a cycle of absolute differences. Which elements of the array can possibly matter for the maximum?
Sort the array. The best cycle alternates small and large values: smallest, largest, second smallest, second largest.
Sort a; print 2·(a[n−1] + a[n−2] − a[0] − a[1]). O(n log n) per test.

codeforces:1985D.title: 1985D · Manhattan Circle
levels: A Manhattan circle on a grid is a diamond. Where is a diamond widest, and how does that relate to its centre?
The centre row is halfway between the topmost and bottommost rows containing '#'; in that row, the centre column is halfway along the '#' segment.

1. top, bottom = first and last rows containing '#'; r = (top + bottom) / 2.
2. In row r, left and right = first and last '#'; c = (left + right) / 2.
3. Print r c (1-indexed). O(nm).

codeforces:1955C.title: 1955C · Inhabitant of the Deep Sea
levels: k can be 10^15, so you cannot simulate attack by attack. How many attacks hit the front in total, and how many hit the back?

The front receives ⌈k/2⌉ attacks and the back ⌊k/2⌋, independently of order. The front sinks the longest prefix with sum ≤ ⌈k/2⌉; the back sinks the longest suffix with sum ≤ ⌊k/2⌋. If k ≥ Σa every ship sinks.

1. If k ≥ Σa print n.
2. front = (k + 1) / 2, back = k / 2.
3. Count prefix ships while the running sum ≤ front; count suffix ships while the running sum ≤ back; print the total. O(n).

codeforces:1923C.title: 1923C · Find B
levels: Every element must change but stay positive. Elements equal to 1 can only go up — where does the extra amount come from?
Each 1 needs at least +1; every element x > 1 can drop to 1 and free x − 1. A subarray is good iff its length is > 1 and Σ(c_i − 1) ≥ the number of ones.
Precompute prefix sums of c and of the count of ones. For a query: len = r − l + 1, s = sum, ones = count. Print YES iff len > 1 and s − len ≥ ones. O(n + q).

codeforces:1991C.title: 1991C · Absolute Zero
levels: Think about parity: what does one operation do to the parities of the elements relative to each other?

If both parities appear, it is impossible — the operation keeps all elements' parities equal to each other or not. Otherwise always pick x = (max + min) / 2: the new maximum is at most half the old range, so about 30 steps suffice.

1. If parities are mixed print −1.
2. Repeat up to 40 times: if all are zero stop; x = (max + min) / 2; record x; a_i = |a_i − x|.
3. Print the recorded operations. O(40·n).

codeforces:1637C.title: 1637C · Andrew and Stones
levels: Every useful operation removes two stones from the middle piles. How many operations does a middle pile of size a need if nothing is wasted?
The answer is Σ⌈a_i/2⌉ over the middle piles, as long as some pile can supply a stone to fix the odd ones. It is impossible if every middle pile is 1, or n = 3 and a_2 is odd.

1. If n == 3 and a_2 is odd → −1.
2. If all of a_2..a_{n−1} are 1 → −1.
3. Otherwise print Σ ⌈a_i/2⌉ for i = 2..n−1 (64-bit). O(n).

codeforces:1760C.title: 1760C · Advantage
levels: For every participant you need the maximum of everyone else. Do you really have to recompute it n times?
Only the maximum and the second maximum matter: everyone compares against the maximum, except the holder of the maximum, who compares against the second maximum.
Find the top two values m1 ≥ m2 (duplicates count separately). For each i print s_i − (s_i == m1 ? m2 : m1). If the maximum appears twice, m2 == m1 and that answer is 0. O(n).

codeforces:2061A.title: 2061A · Kevin and Arithmetic
levels: After Kevin earns a point, s is divided until it becomes odd. Track only parity: which numbers can turn an odd s into an even one?
Put one even number first: s becomes even and scores. From then on s is odd, so every odd number scores and even numbers never do. With no even number at all, the first odd number cannot score.
c1 = number of odd elements. If there is at least one even element print c1 + 1, otherwise print c1 − 1. O(n).
